title: Supernovae and Star Stuff
objective: After this level you can explain how massive stars explode and scatter the elements we are made of.
summary: Stars over ~8 Suns’ mass end in core-collapse supernovae, spreading the elements forged in stars, including those in us.

cards.headline: The iron in your blood was made inside a star.
cards.body: Not a metaphor. To see how it got from there to you, follow a star much more massive than the Sun to its very loud ending.

cards.headline: Going out with a bang
cards.body: Stars more than about eight times as massive as the Sun don’t fade quietly like the white dwarfs of Level 68. Their cores collapse, and the collapse triggers a supernova, an explosion that can briefly outshine an entire galaxy. For a moment, one dying star can be brighter than all its neighbors put together.

cards.headline: Cosmic recycling
cards.body: Nearly all the elements heavier than hydrogen and helium were made by nuclear reactions inside stars and in stellar explosions. Supernovae scatter them into space, where they become part of new stars, planets and people. The calcium in your bones and the iron in your blood were made in stars that lived and died before the Sun formed. You are, quite literally, secondhand star.

mascot.line: If you remember one thing from this level, make it this: the heavy elements in you were made in stars.

cards.fact: In 1987, a supernova was visible to the naked eye.
cards.context: It exploded in the Large Magellanic Cloud, a small galaxy near the Milky Way. No telescope required: a star in another galaxy blew up, and anyone under a dark enough sky could watch.

cards.headline: Star stuff: traced
learned: Stars over ~8 Suns end in core-collapse supernovae
Heavy elements are forged in stars
Supernovae scatter them into new stars and planets
Your bones and blood contain star-made elements

questions.prompt: Which stars end their lives in core-collapse supernovae?

options.label: All stars, including the Sun
options.rationale: The Sun will become a white dwarf instead.

options.label: Stars more than about eight times the Sun’s mass
Only stars that have planets
options.rationale: Planets don’t decide a star’s fate.

questions.explanation: Stars more than about eight times as massive as the Sun end in core-collapse supernovae.

questions.prompt: Where did most of the elements in your body come from?

options.label: They were made by the Big Bang alone
options.rationale: The Big Bang made mostly hydrogen and helium.

options.label: They were forged inside stars and spread by stellar explosions
They formed on Earth’s surface over time
options.rationale: Elements are made in stars, not on planets.

options.label: They arrived on comets only recently
options.rationale: Comets carry elements; they didn’t make them.

questions.explanation: Heavier elements, like the calcium in bones and the iron in blood, were made in stars and scattered by supernovae.

questions.prompt: From Level 32: how do astronomers know which elements a supernova blasted out?

options.label: They measure how loud the explosion was
They time how long it stays bright
They read the spectral lines in its light

questions.explanation: Each element leaves its own spectral lines, so a supernova’s spectrum reveals what it contains.
